title: the crossing of the Yamuna
hook: the guards fall asleep, the bolted doors swing open, and Vasudeva walks out into a storm carrying a newborn

segments.voice: Yesterday, the birth: four arms at midnight, and then, at Devaki's request, an ordinary baby on the prison floor. Your line was he becomes small enough to hold. What small moment did you treat as precious? Day eight hundred eighty-two, the end of a week.

The baby has only just been born, and he cannot stay. Kamsa's guards are just outside. The Bhagavata says that Vasudeva, prompted by the Lord himself, picks up his son. And then the prison starts to come undone. The guards slump into sleep. The doors, bolted and barred with iron, open on their own, the way darkness gives way to the sun. Outside, rain is falling and the clouds rumble low. Somewhere ahead, in the dark, is the river. Today Vasudeva walks out of the prison with his son.
screen: `A NEWBORN SON.` → `THE GUARDS SLEEP.` → `THE DOORS OPEN BY THEMSELVES.`

segments.voice: Notice who does what. The miracles open the way, but they don't carry the child. Vasudeva does that, in his own arms, through a storm, at night. The Bhagavata adds two details. First, the rain. As Vasudeva walks, Shesha, the great serpent on whom Vishnu rests, follows behind him and spreads his hoods over the father and child like an umbrella. The cosmic serpent, holding off the weather for a newborn. Then the river. The Yamuna that night is swollen and fast, the text says, full of waves and whirlpools and foam, deep enough to stop anyone. And the river makes way. The Bhagavata compares it to the ocean giving way for Rama, when he crossed to Lanka to bring back Sita. The same Lord, another age, another stretch of water opening. Later retellings add more. In some, Vasudeva carries the baby in a basket on his head; in some, the river rises to touch the child's feet before it parts. Those details belong to the retellings; the Bhagavata's own account is shorter: the father, the child, the serpent, the river giving way. Look back over this week and it has the same shape again and again. Yudhishthira refusing to leave a dog. Yudhishthira staying in the dark with his family. Vasudeva keeping a terrible promise. Now Vasudeva, walking into a flood with a baby. Help arrives in this week's stories, but someone still has to walk.
screen: `THE FATHER CARRIES THE CHILD` · `SHESHA SPREADS HIS HOODS` · `THE RIVER GIVES WAY` · then, large: `SOMEONE STILL HAS TO WALK`

segments.voice: Sit, and let your feet rest flat on the floor. Feel their weight. Vasudeva crossed on foot. Breathe in, and bring to mind something you are carrying right now for someone else, a worry, a task, a person who depends on you. Breathe out, and notice what has been holding off the rain for you: a friend, a habit, a faith, a bit of luck. Let yourself see both, the carrying and the shelter. If you pray, you can give thanks in your own way. The bell holds the time.
Shesha. The great serpent on whom Vishnu rests, who spreads his hoods over Vasudeva and the newborn child in the storm.
Your line: the river gives way. Today, thank one person who has been holding off the rain for you. That's the week: a dog, a dark place, a promise, a river. Day eight hundred eighty-two.

screen: `DAY 882 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE CROSSING OF THE YAMUNA.`

howItsDone: The crossing of the Yamuna is retold at Janmashtami in songs, plays and temple tableaux, and the image of Vasudeva carrying the infant through the river under Shesha's hoods is a familiar one in Hindu art.

pairs: spreads his hoods against the rain
gives way, as the ocean did for Rama

myth: in the Bhagavata, the river rises to touch the baby's feet
that comes from later retellings; the Bhagavata simply says the river gave way.
Shesha shelters the father and child from the rain
the serpent follows and spreads his hoods over them.
Vasudeva has to break down the prison doors
the bolted doors open on their own.

fork.setup: you're Vasudeva. the doors are open, it's pouring, and the river ahead is in flood. what do you do?
options: wait in the prison for the storm to pass.
walk out into the storm with the baby.
hide the baby somewhere in the city.
fork.reveal: he walks out at once, and Shesha shelters him while the Yamuna makes way.

original.note: shesha: the great serpent on whom Vishnu rests, who shelters the child in the storm.

trapdoor: what you thought: the river miraculously carried the baby across.
what it means: the river makes way, but Vasudeva carries his son himself, on foot, through the storm.
what a scholar hears: the Bhagavata compares the river to the ocean giving way for Rama, tying this night to another of Vishnu's descents.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 10.3.47–50: Vasudeva takes the child, the guards sleep, the doors open, Shesha shelters them, the Yamuna gives way as the ocean did for Rama

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm verse range 10.3.47–50 and the simile of doors opening as darkness yields to the sun.
The script says the basket and the river touching the child's feet come from later retellings and are not in the Bhagavata's account; a Keeper should confirm this and the myth item built on it.
